landing.guide_title: A short guide to paying off debt

guide.h: What is the debt snowball method?
p: With the snowball method you list your debts from the smallest balance to the largest. You pay the minimum on every debt and put any extra money toward the smallest one. When it is paid off, its payment rolls into the next, so your payoff power grows with every debt you clear.
Its biggest strength is momentum: the first debt disappears within months, which makes the plan easier to stick with.

guide.h: What is the debt avalanche method?
p: With the avalanche method you list your debts from the highest interest rate to the lowest. The extra money goes to the most expensive debt first. Because you clear the debt that grows the fastest, this method usually costs the least interest overall.
The trade-off: if your highest-rate debt is large, the first payoff can take a while.

guide.h: Which one is right for you?
p: The difference is often small; having a plan is what matters most. The calculator above compares both methods with your numbers and shows which one costs less.

guide.h: How the math works, with an example
p: Each month, interest is charged first: the balance times the monthly rate. A $5,000 credit card balance at 24% APR, which is 2% a month, is charged $100 of interest that month.
Then every debt gets its minimum payment and the extra goes to the next debt in line. When a debt is paid off, its payment rolls over to the next one.
The calculator repeats these steps month by month until the last debt is gone; that gives your debt-free month and the total interest you pay.

guide.h: The minimum payment trap
p: Paying only the minimum on a credit card keeps the debt alive: interest is charged on the rest every month and the balance can last for years.
Even a small amount on top of the minimum moves your debt-free date months closer. Try it with your own numbers in the extra payment section above.

guide.h: Ways to get out of debt faster
list: Stop adding new debt: use the card only for what you can pay off within the month.
Pay a fixed amount above the minimums every month, and automate it.
Send bonuses, refunds and side income straight to the next debt in line.
Work out whether moving a high-rate balance to a lower-rate loan really costs less overall.
Review your subscriptions; cancel the ones you don't use and put the difference toward your debt.
Never miss a due date: late fees and penalty rates push your plan back.

faq.q: Does the snowball or the avalanche method cost less interest?
faq.a: In most cases the avalanche method, paying the highest interest rate first, costs the least interest overall. The snowball method clears your first debt sooner, which keeps you motivated. The calculator compares both with your numbers.

faq.q: Which debts can I add?

faq.q: Where do I find my interest rate?
faq.a: It is on your credit card statement, in your loan agreement or in your bank's app, usually shown as the APR. Enter the APR; the calculator works out the monthly rate.

faq.q: How accurate is the result?
faq.a: It assumes your rates stay the same, you pay the same amount every month and there are no extra fees. Real rates can change, so use the result as a plan, not a quote.

faq.q: Is anything I enter sent anywhere?
faq.a: No. The math runs entirely in your browser; nothing you enter is saved or sent anywhere.

faq.q: What does Spendry do that this calculator doesn't?
faq.a: Spendry works with your real balances, updates the plan after every payment, reminds you before each due date and always shows the day you'll be debt-free. It never asks for your bank login and collects no data.

guide.h: What is the 50/30/20 rule?
p: Half of your take-home pay goes to needs (rent, bills, groceries, transport), 30 percent to wants (eating out, entertainment, shopping) and 20 percent to savings and paying off debt.
It is a starting point. If rent alone takes half of your income, adjust the split to fit your life, and pay off high-interest debt first.

guide.h: How to make a monthly budget
p: Start with your income: salary, side jobs and any other regular money. Then set aside the fixed costs at the start of the month: rent, bills, loan payments and subscriptions.

Record variable spending like groceries, eating out and transport as it happens; left to the end of the month, most of it is forgotten. At the end of the month, subtract spending from income and move what is left to savings.

guide.h: Plan for your credit card statement
p: Card purchases don't leave your account today; they come out when you pay the statement. When you plan the month, count the statement you will pay, not just today's balance.

guide.h: Ways to stick to a budget
list: Pay yourself first: move savings out as soon as you are paid.
Enter fixed costs once and let them repeat every month.
Record small purchases too; they make the biggest difference by the end of the month.
Review your subscriptions once a year.
Check your budget in the middle of the month and adjust the second half if you need to.

faq.q: Does the 50/30/20 rule work for everyone?

faq.q: Should I use my gross or net income?

landing.guide_title: A short guide to credit card debt

guide.h: How credit card interest is calculated
p: Each month your card charges interest on the balance you carry, based on its APR. Your payment covers that interest first, and the rest reduces the balance. The calculator repeats this month by month until the balance is gone.
Example: a $3,000 balance at 24% APR, which is 2% a month, is charged $60 of interest. Pay $200 and the balance drops to $2,860; next month's interest is worked out on that new amount.

guide.h: Why minimum payments take so long
p: The minimum payment is usually a small percentage of the balance. As the balance falls, so does the minimum, so most of each payment goes to interest and the debt can last for years.
Paying a fixed amount breaks that cycle: the same money keeps shrinking the balance every month. The comparison in the calculator shows the difference with your numbers.

guide.h: Statement date and due date
p: The statement date closes the billing cycle and sets your balance. The due date is the last day to pay it, usually at least 21 days later.
Pay the full statement balance by the due date and you are not charged interest on purchases. Carry part of it and interest is charged on what is left.

guide.h: Ways to pay off a card faster

Pause new spending on the card while you pay it down.
If you have several cards, put the extra toward the highest APR first.
Check whether a balance transfer or a lower-rate loan really costs less once fees are included.
Never miss a due date; late fees and penalty rates push your plan back.
